<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{Th1}
		Let $ f(x), g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be two monic polynomials such that $(f\circ g)(x)$ is irreducible. Then $$I^{\deg g}_f ~ \text{ divides }~ I_{f\circ g}.$$
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{C1}
		Let $ f(x), g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be two monic polynomials such that $(f\circ g)(x)$ is irreducible. If $L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(g(\theta))$, where $(f\circ g)(\theta)=0,$ then $[\mathbb{Z}_K:\mathbb{Z}[g(\theta)]]^{[L:K]}$ divides  $[\mathbb{Z}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\theta]].$
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
In general for any tower $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K\subseteq L$ of number fields, this result does not hold. For example, if $L=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[8]{3})$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, where $\alpha=1+2\sqrt[4]{3}+\sqrt{3}$ then $[\mathbb{Z}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt[8]{3}]]=1$ and $[\mathbb{Z}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]=112.$ Clearly $[\mathbb{Z}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]\nmid [\mathbb{Z}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt[8]{3}]].$
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Let $ f(x),g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be two monic polynomials such that $(f\circ g)(x)$ is irreducible. If $p$ is a prime such that $v_{p}(I_{f\circ g})< \deg g$, then $p$ does not divide $I_f.$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Let $f(x)=x^6+x-12$ and $g(x)=x^6-2.$ Then the polynomial $(f\circ g)(x)=x^{36} - 12x^{30} + 60x^{24} - 160x^{18} + 240x^{12} - 191x^6 + 50$ is irreducible. Here, $I_{f\circ g}=2^3\times 5^3.$ Take $L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, where $(f\circ g)(\theta)=0.$ As $v_p(I_{f\circ g})<\deg g$ for any prime $p$, therefore in view of the above corollary $I_f=1.$
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{C11}
		Let $p$ be a prime and $t$ be a positive integer. Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial such that $f(x^{p^t})$ is irreducible. If $f(x)$ is monogenic and $|f(0)|=1,$ then the index of $f(x^{p^t})$ is equal to $p^s,$ for some non-negative integer $s.$
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{Th3}
		Let $ f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $d$ such that $f^n(x)$ is irreducible for every $n\in\mathbb{N}.$ Then the following statements are true:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item $I_n$ divides  $I_{n+1}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}.$
			\item If $m\le n$, then  $I_m^{d^{n-m}}$ divides  $I_n$.
			\item $\langle I_{n}\rangle$ is an increasing sequence.
			\item The iterate $f^n(x)$ is monogenic for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ if and only if  the sequence $\langle I_{n} \rangle$ is bounded.
			                                                                                                        
			                                                     
			                                                                                                                                 
			\item If $I_n$ is $d^{\text{th}}$ power free integer, then $I_m=1$ for each $m<n$.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{C12}
		Let $ f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial such that $f^n(x)$ is irreducible for all $n\in\mathbb{N}.$ Then $f^n(x)$ is monogenic for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ if and only if $\langle I_n \rangle$ is convergent.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{P6}
			Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $d\ge 2$ such that the $n^{\text{th}}$ iterate $f^n(x)$ is irreducible. Let $\theta_n$ be a root of $f^n(x)$ and let $\theta_i=f(\theta_{i+1})$. If $I_n$ is $m^{\text{th}}$ power free integer, then at least $\max\{\lfloor n-\log_dm \rfloor,0\}$ fields in the following tower are monogenic. $$\mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathbb{Q}(\theta_1)\subseteq \cdots\subseteq\mathbb{Q}(\theta_{n-1})\subseteq\mathbb{Q}(\theta_n).$$
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
If $m=\deg f$ or $m=2$ in the above corollary, then $ \lfloor n- \log_{\deg f} m \rfloor= n-1$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{Th2}
					Let $ f(x),g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be two monic polynomials such that $g(x)$ and $(f\circ g)(x)$ are irreducible. If $(f\circ g)(x)$ is monogenic, then $\gcd\large(I^2_g,f(0)\large)$ is square-free.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let $f(x)=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+25$ and $g(x)=x^3-25$, then $I_f=1$ and $I_g=5.$ Note that $f(x)$ is monogenic. Here $\gcd (I_g^2,f(0))=25$, not a square-free integer. Therefore from the above theorem $(f\circ g)(x)$ is non-monogenic.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{L2.1}
		 If   $I$ and $J$ are non-zero fractional ideals in $L$, then the following statements are true.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item If $I \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_L$, then $N_{L/K}(I) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_K$.
			\item If $I \subseteq J$, then $N_{L/K}(I) \subseteq N_{L/K}(J)$.
			\item If $I$ is a principal fractional ideal generated by $a \in L$, then $N_{L/K}(I)$ is the principal fractional ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_K$ generated by $\mathcal{N}_{L/K}(a)$.
			\item The ideal $d_{K/\mathbb{Q}}$ is generated by $d_K$.
			\item If $I \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_K$, then $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(I)$ is the principal ideal generated by $N(I)$, where $N(I)$ is the absolute norm of $I$.
			\item   $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(I)=N(I)\mathbb{Z}.$
			                                                                                                           
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{pth2}
		The different $D_{L/K} $ is generated as an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_L$ by the set of all differents \[ \delta_{L/K}(\alpha)=
		\begin{cases}
			f'(\alpha), & ~ \text{ if } L=K(\alpha) \text{ with minimal polynomial } f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}_K[x],\\
			0, & ~ \text{ otherwise },
		\end{cases}	\] with $\alpha$ running over $\mathbb{Z}_L.$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{L2.3}
		If $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K\subseteq L$ is a tower of number fields, then $d_{L/\mathbb{Q}}=d_{K/\mathbb{Q}}^{[L:K]}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L/K}).$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{L2.5}
		Let $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K\subseteq L$ be a tower of number fields such that $L$ is generated by $\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_L$ over $K.$ If $g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}_K[x]$ is the minimal polynomial of $\theta,$ then the absolute norm of the ideal  $D_{L/K}$  divides the absolute value of $\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\alpha)).$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Here $L=K(\theta)$ and $g(x)$ is the minimal polynomial of $\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_L$ over $K.$ From Theorem \ref{pth2}, we have 
		$D_{L/K}= \langle\{ \delta_{L/K}(\alpha) ~ ~ | ~~ \alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_L\}\rangle.$ This shows that
		$g'(\theta)\in D_{L/K}$ and therefore $ 
		g'(\theta)\mathbb{Z}_L\subseteq D_{L/K}.$ Using $(2)$ of Lemma \ref{L2.1}, we see that \begin{equation}\label{EQa}
			N_{L/K}(g'(\theta)\mathbb{Z}_L)\subseteq N_{L/K}(D_{L/K}).
		\end{equation} Using $(3)$ of Lemma \ref{L2.1}, we get $N_{L/K}(g'(\theta)\mathbb{Z}_L)=\mathcal{N}_{L/K}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}_K$. By $\eqref{EQa}$ and in view of the fact that $\mathbb{Z}_K$ is a Dedekind domain,  we can write 
		\begin{equation}\label{EQb}
			\mathcal{N}_{L/K}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}_K=N_{L/K}(D_{L/K})C ,\end{equation} for some ideal $C$ of $\mathbb{Z}_K.$ Apply norm $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}$ on both side of \eqref{EQb}, we obtain 
		$$N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathcal{N}_{L/K}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}_K))=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(N_{L/K}(D_{L/K}))N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(C).$$ Hence by $(3)$ of Lemma \ref{L2.1} and multiplicative property of $\mathcal{N}$, we see that $N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(D_{L/K})$ divides  
		$\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}.$ Write $\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}=N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(D_{L/K})A,$ for some ideal $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}.$ Then by $(6)$ of Lemma \ref{L2.1}, $\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))\mathbb{Z}=N(D_{L/K}))\mathbb{Z} A,$ where $N$ denotes the absolute norm. Using multiplicative property of $N$,  we get$|\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))|=N(D_{L/K})N(A).$ 
		This implies that $N(D_{L/K})$ divides $|\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\alpha))|.$
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemmaB}
		Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be two non-zero monic polynomials belonging to $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that $(f \circ g)(x)$ is irreducible, then the discriminant formula of  $(f\circ g)(x)$ is given by $$D(f\circ g)=\pm D(f)^{\deg g}\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\alpha)),$$ where $\alpha$ is a root of $(f\circ g)(x).$
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{remark}
		Note that if $g(x)=x^{n}$ in the above lemma, then the discriminant formula of $f(x^n)$ is  $$D(f(x^n))=\pm D(f)^{n}n^{n\deg f}f(0)^{n-1}.$$
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{UL}	An  ideal $\mathfrak M$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ containing a monic polynomial is maximal if and only if $\mathfrak M =  \langle p, g(x) \rangle $  for some prime number   $p$  and a monic polynomial  $g(x)$ belonging to $\mathbb Z [x]$ which is irreducible modulo $p$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{UT}
		Let  $K=\mathbb Q(\theta)$  with  $\theta$ in $\mathbb{Z}_K$ having  minimal polynomial $f(x)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, then $\mathbb{Z}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ if and only if $f(x)$ does not belong to $\mathfrak M ^2$ for any maximal ideal $\mathfrak M$ of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Z[x]$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{PL1}
		Let $f(x), g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be two monic polynomials such that  $f\circ g$ is irreducible. Let $h(x)$ be a monic irreducible polynomial modulo a prime $p$ such that $g(x)\in \langle p, h(x) \rangle^2$. Then $$f(g(x))\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2 ~ ~ ~ \iff ~ ~ ~ p^2 \text{ divide } f(0).$$
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $f(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0.$ Then 
			$f(g(x))=g(x)b(x)+a_0,$ where $b(x)=g(x)^{n-1}+a_{n-1}g(x)^{n-2}+\cdots+a_2g(x)+a_1.$ As $h(x)$ is a monic irreducible polynomial modulo $p$ and $g(x)\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2.$ Therefore $g(x)b(x)\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2.$ This shows that $f(g(x))\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2$ if and only if  $a_0\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2.$
		Equivalently, 
		$f(g(x))\in \langle p,h(x)\rangle^2$ if and only if $a_0=p^2u(x)+ph(x)v(x)+h^2(x)w(x),$ for some $u(x),v(x), w(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x].$ This happens only when $p^2$ divides $ f(0)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{PTh1}
		Let $F$ be a field. Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be two monic polynomials belonging to $F[x]$ and $\beta$ be a root of $f(x)$ in the algebraic closure of $F$, then $(f\circ g)(x)$ is irreducible over $F$ if and only if 
		 $f(x)$ is irreducible over $F$ and $g(x)-\beta$ is irreducible over $F(\beta).$
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Set 
		$K=\mathbb{Q}(g(\theta))$,  
		$L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta),$ where
		$(f\circ g)(\theta)=0.$ From Theorem \ref{PTh1}, it is clear that $h(x)=g(x)-g(\theta)\in\mathbb{Z}_K[x]$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_K$ and $h(\theta)=0$. Using Lemmas~\ref{L2.3} and~\ref{lemmaB} we have 
		$$D(f\circ g)=\pm D(f)^{[L:K]}\, \mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}\!\big(g'(\theta)\big) ~ ~ \text{ and } ~ ~ ~
			d_{L/\mathbb{Q}}= d_{K/\mathbb{Q}}^{[L:K]}\, N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L|K}).$$
		\noindent From $(4)$  and $(5)$ of Lemma \ref{L2.1}, we get \begin{equation}\label{eqr}
		d_{L}= \pm d_{K}^{[L:K]}\, N(N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L/K})),\end{equation} where $N(N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L/K}))$ is the absolute norm of $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L/K}).$ Now by well known identities $D(f)=I_f^2d_K$ and $D(f\circ g)=I_{f\circ g}^2d_L$, we see that
		$I_{f \circ g}^2\, d_L
			= \pm D(f)^{[L:K]}\, \mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}\!\big(g'(\theta)\big)$
		Using \eqref{eqr}, we obtain
		$$I_{f\circ g}^2\, d_K^{[L:K]}\, N(N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d_{L|K}))= (I_f^2\, d_K)^{[L:K]}\, \mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}\!\big(g'(\theta)\big).$$ By multiplicative property of norm and $(6)$ of lemma \ref{L2.1}, we get
		$\frac{I_{f\circ g}^2}{I_f^{2[L:K]}}=\frac{
				|\mathcal{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))|
			}{
				N(D_{L/K})
			}.$
		 Since $g'(\theta)\in D_{L/K}$, we see that $N_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(g'(\theta))\in\mathbb{Z}.$ Hence the conclusion follows from Lemma \ref{L2.5}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$(1)$ Let $\theta$ be a root of $F(x):=f(x^{p^t})$ and let $\theta_0=\theta^{p^t}$.  So by Theorem \ref{PTh1}, $[\mathbb{Q}(\theta):\mathbb{Q}(\theta_0)]=p^{t}$. Using Remark \ref{remark} with the well-known identity $D(F)=I_F^2d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}$, we see that \begin{equation*}\label{eqP1}
			D(F(x))=(d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta_0)})^{p^t}p^{tp^t\deg f}=I_F^2d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}.\end{equation*}
		 As $d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta_0)}^{p^t}$ divides $d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)},$ therefore $I_F=p^s$, for some non-negative integer $s.$
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$(1)$ Here $f^{n+1}(x)=(f\circ f\circ \cdots\circ f)\circ f(x)=f^n(f(x)).$ Let $L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(f^n(\theta)),$ where $\theta$ is a root of $f^{n+1}(x).$ Clearly from Theorem \ref{PTh1}, $f(x)-f(\theta)$ is irreducible over $K$ and so $[L:K]=\deg f=d.$ By Theorem \ref{Th1}, we conclude that $I_{f^n\circ f}$ is divisible by $I_f^d.$ \\
		$(2)$ From the above case, we see that $I^d_n$ divides $I_{n+1}$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}.$ Let $m\le n.$ Then the degree of $f^m(x)$ and $f^n(x)$ is $d^m$ and $d^n$ respectively. Set $n=m+t.$ Let $K_{m+i}=\mathbb{Q}(f^{t-i}(\theta))$ for $0\le i\le t-1$ and $L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$,  where $\theta$ is a root of $f^n(x)$.  Clearly we have the following tower of number fields. $$K_m\subseteq K_{m+1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq K_{n-1}\subseteq L.$$ From Theorem \ref{PTh1}, $[K_{m+i+1}:K_{m+i}]=\deg f=d$. A simple induction shows that $I_m^{d^t}$ divides $I_n.$\\
		$(3)$ Clearly from the above case, the sequence $\langle I_n\rangle$ is an increasing sequence.\\
		$(4)$ First suppose that $f^n(x)$ is monogenic for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.  Then $I_n=1$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}.$ So $I_n$ is bounded.  Conversely, let there exist a positive real number $M$ such that $I_n\le M$  for all $n\in\mathbb{N}.$ Suppose for some $m\in \mathbb{N},$ the $m$-fold composition $f^m(x)$ of $f(x)$ is non-monogenic, then $I_m>1$ and $\deg f^m(x)=d^m.$ Since $M$ is fix, we can easily choose a natural number $t$ such that $I_m^t>M.$ For a suitable natural number $u>t$ we obtain $I_m^{d^u}>I_m^t.$ By Case (2), we get $I_m^{d^u}\mid I_{m+u}$ and so $I_{m+u}>M$, a contradiction. Hence for all $n,$ the $n^{\text{th}}$ iterate $f^n(x)$ is monogenic.\\
		$(5)$ Here $I_n$ is $d^{\text{th}}$ power free integer. Suppose for some $m<n,$ $I_m>1.$ Then using Case $(2)$, $I_m^{d^{n-m}}\mid I_n$, which is not possible. So $I_m=1$ for all $m<n.$
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
First suppose that $f^n(x)$ is monogenic for all $n\in\mathbb{N}.$ Then $I_n=1$ for all $n.$ Therefore the sequence $\langle I_n \rangle$ is convergent. Conversely, suppose $\langle I_n \rangle$ is convergent. Since $I_n$ is a sequence of natural number so it must be eventually constant, i.e., there exist some natural numbers $c$ and $N$ such that $I_n=c ~ ~  \text{ for all } n\ge N.$ Now using $(2)$ of Theorem \ref{Th3}, $I_{N}^{\deg f}$ divides $I_{N+1}.$ That is, $c^{\deg f}$ divides $c.$ This happens only when $c=1.$ Thus $I_n=1$ for all $n\ge N.$ Next, using $(5)$ of Theorem \ref{Th3}, we see that $I_n=1$ for all $n<N.$ Hence for all $n\in\mathbb{N},$ the $n^{\text{th}}$ iterate $f^n(x)$ is monogenic.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $k\le n$. Clearly from $(2)$ of Theorem \ref{Th3} we have  $I_k^{d^{n-k}}\mid I_n.$ For $I_k=1,$ we let $d^{n-k} \ge m$. Then we have $d^{n}\ge md^k>1.$ This implies that $n\log d\ge \log m +k\log d.$ So we get $n\log d- \log m \ge k\log d,$ i.e., $n- \log_d m \ge k.$ This means that $k= \lfloor n- \log_d m \rfloor,$ where $\lfloor a \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $a.$
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that $\gcd(I_g^2,f(0))$ is not square-free. Let $p$ be a prime dividing $\gcd(I_g^2,f(0))$, then by Lemma \ref{UL} and Theorem \ref{UT}, $g(x)\in \langle p, h(x)\rangle^2$ for some monic irreducible factor $h(x)$ of $g(x)$ modulo $p.$ From Lemma \ref{PL1}, we known that $f(g(x))\in \langle p, h(x)\rangle^2$ if and only if  $p^2\mid f(0).$ As $p^2\mid f(0)$, so $h(x)$ is also an irreducible factor of $f(g(x))$ modulo $p$. Thus by Lemma \ref{UL} and Theorem \ref{UT}, we conclude that $p\mid I_{f\circ g}.$
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
Let $k\ge 2$ be a positive integer. Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial such that $f(x^k)$ is irreducible. If $f(x^k)$ is monogenic, then \begin{enumerate}
			\item $f(x)$ is monogenic,
			\item $p$ does not divide the index of $f(x^{p})$ for any prime $p\mid k$, and 
			\item $f(0)$ is square-free.
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
First suppose that $F(x)$ is monogenic. Using Theorem \ref{Th1}, we see that each $f(x^p)$  is monogenic and $f(x)$ is also monogenic. Using Lemma \ref{PL1} together with Theorem \ref{UT}, we can easily observe that $f(0)$ must be square-free.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
Let $k\ge 2$ be a positive integer. Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ be a monic polynomial such that $f(x^k)$ is irreducible. If  \begin{enumerate}
			\item $f(x)$ is monogenic,
			\item $p$ does not divide the index of $f(x^{p^{v_p(k)}})$ for any prime $p\mid k$, and 
			\item $|f(0)|=1$,
		\end{enumerate} then $f(x^k)$ is monogenic.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Write $k=p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots p_t^{e_t}$ as a product of distinct  prime powers. Let $k_i=\frac{k}{p_i^{e_i}}$ for $1\le i\le t$. Set $F_i(x)=f(x^{p_i^{e_i}})$. Then $F(x):=f(x^k)=F_i(x^{k_i})$ for all $1\le i\le t.$ Clearly from Theorem \ref{PTh1}, each $F_i$ is irreducible. Suppose that $\theta$ is a root of $F(x)$, then $F_i(\theta^{k_i})=0$ and $f(\theta^k)=0.$ Let $\theta_i=\theta^{k_i}$, then $[\mathbb{Q}(\theta):\mathbb{Q}(\theta_i)]=k_i$ for all $i=1,2\ldots,t.$
		
		In view of Remark \ref{remark} and the fact that $D(F(x))=I_F^2d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}$, we have \begin{align*}I_F^2d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}&=\pm D(F_i)^{k_i}k_i^{k\deg f},\\
			&=\pm I^{2k_i}_{F_i}(d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta_i)})^{k_i}k_i^{k\deg f}.	\end{align*} 
		Clearly Theorem \ref{Th1}, implies that $I_{F_i}^{2k_i}$ divides $I_F^2$. Also we know that  $d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta_i)}^{k_i}$ divides $d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}$.
		Using Corollary \ref{C11} and given condition (2), for each $i$ we have $I_{F_i}=1$. Also, for each $1\le i\le t,$ $k_i=\frac{k}{p_i^{e_i}}$ implies that $p_i$ does not divide $I_F.$ Thus any prime divisor of $k$ will not divide $I_F.$ Therefore the identity $I^2_Fd_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta)}=\pm I^{2k}_{f}(d_{\mathbb{Q}(\theta_k)})^{k}k^{k\deg f}$ implies that $I_F=1.$
<!-- end proof-10 -->
